newsitem.title: USA: Energy Department seek $19.2 billion for 1998.
newsitem.headline: Energy Department seek $19.2 billion for 1998.

text.p: The Energy Department proposed spending $16.6 billion in the 1998 fiscal year but Thursday asked Congress for $19.2 billion for 1998 including planned future costs.

The core budget plan was $400 million or 2.6 percent higher than the department's 1997 budget. More than half the increase was devoted to energy efficiency and renewable energy programmes, with the rest split between preserving the nation's nuclear stockpile without testing and nuclear waste cleanup.
More than two-thirds of the department's budget would go towards nuclear weapons programmes and waste cleanup.
Despite Republicans' attempts to cut spending and get rid of the department, Congress last year gave the department a bigger budget than the administration sought.

"The 104th Congress, which struggled so mightily with fiscal matters, I'd like to point out, also increased this department's budget," Acting Deputy Energy Secretary Charles Curtis said at a news conference.
The $2.6 billion in future costs included in the 1998 budget request were for construction spending for nuclear programmes and contracts for cleaning up weapons facilities.

Although the department ended its funding of research into an advanced light water reactor for nuclear power plants, long slammed by anti-nuclear groups, the agency added a new $40 million programme focused on commercial nuclear power.
It is a "new effort to address nuclear power plant-ageing issues and develop technology to reduce spent fuel," the department said.
"In our minds this is just another example of corporate welfare for the nuclear industry," said Scott Denman, executive director of the Safe Energy Communication Council.
The department's 1998 request for energy efficiency and renewable energy programmes totalled $1.02 billion, up from $840 million approved by Congress for this year.

While clean energy advocates applauded the increase, Congressional aides doubted it would be approved. "We've not approved their (energy conservation) budgets in the past. They're trying to ... short-change fossil (fuels), and boost energy efficiency," said one Republican aide.
Fossil energy research and development was slated for a cut from $365 million in 1997 to a request of $346 million for 1998, including a $17 million cut in natural gas research.

Curtis said the Energy Department was well on track towards meeting a goal set two years ago by then Secretary Hazel O'Leary to cut the agency's spending by $10 billion over four years through asset sales, shifts in research priorities, lower cleanup contract costs, and staff cuts.

The original aim was to cut spending by $14 billion, with a selloff of the federal hydropower marketing agencies. However, once Congress rejected the plan, the administration decided not to propose it again.
